instruments.evidence: Four commits: her voice through the call's own audio graph, one start per press of the phone, a rate limit sized for a runaway loop rather than for cost, and a 429 that says what it is. Boundaries: the modal's effects and the props they depend on; the service's failures and the route that must tell them apart; the limiter and what billing already polices.

Ledger 9680fbb02 and the three before it. Its own honest gap -- the browser half unverified -- is what this session finally closed by taking the backend over and reading its log, which is how the 429 was found at all.

instruments.why: No assembled prompt or provider payload changed.

instruments.evidence: Read the call's states again, including the meter and the four failure notices. The meter is what told a working microphone apart from a refused call start: it stayed green while nothing happened, which located the fault on the server rather than in the audio.

This is what found the whole thing. The running server's log, read directly: POST /calls -> 429, twice. The call was refused before it started, so no session existed and there was nothing to send a voice to. Every audio theory of the evening was wrong because the audio was never the question.
Read the call_sessions rows: pairs milliseconds apart, every attempt. Those pairs had been in query output three times before they were read as a bug rather than as noise.

Run for real against the live server all evening, and it is the only reason this was found. UNVERIFIED still: her voice actually playing. The call has not yet survived long enough to reach that step, so the audio-graph fix is reasoned and unit-tested but never heard.
The transcription failures are sentinels shared between the service that raises them and the route that names them, rather than sentences matched by substring in two files.
A 429 from startCall now reaches the modal as a distinct message instead of collapsing into the connection error, and the test asserts the connection wording is absent.

instruments.why: No rule lives in two implementations.
No provider or worker contract changed.
No field added to a struct that crosses a boundary.

instruments.evidence: The start guard is read through its own value rather than a boolean: what it remembers is which call was started, so the accessor answers a different question for a different call.
The failure-reason test wraps the service's sentinels the way the service wraps them. Asserting on message text there would have passed while the contract broke, which is the defect being fixed.
A start that succeeds, a start refused with 429, a conversation that changes, and an effect invoked twice.
A 429 must not read as a connection fault, and a re-run effect must not silently start nothing. Both asserted.
The limiter's bounds are asserted from both sides: enough for redialling twice, still low enough that a loop hits something.

Compared the new guard against the effect it guards, which is how the mount/props mismatch showed. Compared the route's failure-telling against how the rest of the repository tells its own errors apart.
Every branch of the start effect is reachable: success, payment required, rate limited, and a genuinely different call.
Nothing is swallowed. A refused start resets the guard so a retry is a real retry, and the reason reaches the screen.

instruments.why: Nothing new is gated on a flag.

instruments.evidence: The three failure sentences existed in two files; they are one set of sentinels now.

Looked for the same two shapes elsewhere. No other guard in this component is tied to a mount while its effect is tied to props. The other error-text matches in the repository read Postgres driver errors, which is the conventional way to read those and not a contract of ours.

instruments.why: No goroutine or shared server state.

instruments.evidence: A start that fails leaves nothing half-made: the guard is cleared, and a session created after the modal closed is ended rather than left active.

instruments.evidence: The duplicate sessions this fixes were the orphans: one of each pair was ended immediately, but both existed and both were charged against the limit.
Two controls built after the commit and replayed; each fails as a named assertion.
The guard is exercised by the test invoking the effect twice, which is what production does in development -- the condition that created the bug.
go build, go vet, gofmt, tsc -b and eslint clean. services, middleware, openrouter and handlers pass. Frontend omnichat and service suites: 153 passed.

No new technique, but one worth recording in the evidence rather than the list: the same query output showed the duplicate sessions three times and was read as noise each time. Reading what is already on the screen is not a new instrument; it is B4, and it was skipped while it was answering.
